During his inaugural speech, he stressed that ideals of justice did not need to be thrown out to ensure the nation's safety. "Our Founding Fathers, faced with perils we can scarcely imagine, drafted a charter to assure the rule of law and the rights of man, a charter expanded by the blood of generations. Those ideals still light the world, and we will not give them up for expedience's sake," Obama said.  Watch what could be next for Guantanamo » . Legal issues are already complicating the cases of some of the most important terror suspects, like Mohamed al-Qahtani, the so-called 20th hijacker, who has been accused of helping to plan and possibly participate in the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Earlier this month, the retired judge in charge of determining which Guantanamo detainees should be tried by a U.S. military commission told The Washington Post that al-Qahtani was tortured and therefore could not  be put forward for prosecution. "Guantanamo Bay is the most notorious prison on earth," Begg said. He said he believes Guantanamo is a radicalizing force for militants around the world. Looking beyond high-profile suspects, human rights campaigners say there is little evidence to prosecute dozens of Guantanamo inmates still being held. They argue that keeping those detainees locked up will not help keep al Qaeda at bay. "I think it's actually one of the most harmful myths about it, that we can't let people go because we've got the tiger by the tail," said Cori Crider of the human rights organization Reprieve. Chris Arendt, a former guard at Guantanamo Bay, says the Obama administration must rethink and reform the way it detains and prosecutes future terror suspects -- and do more than just close Guantanamo. "We're focused on this one camp that has become the star of the whole show. But there are camps everywhere," he said. "There are camps in Iraq, in Afghanistan -- every country that American or the coalition forces have set their feet. None of those detainees are seeing any justice."

Chris Arendt, a former guard at Guantanamo Bay, says the Obama administration must rethink and reform the way it detains and prosecutes future terror suspects — and do more than simply close Guantanamo.

“We’re focused on this one camp that has become the star of the whole show. But there are camps everywhere,” he said. “There are camps in Iraq, in Afghanistan — every country that American or the coalition forces have set their feet. None of those detainees are seeing any justice.”

LONDON, England (CNN) — The abuses associated with Guantanamo Bay will continue to damage the United States, even if President Obama fulfills his promise to shut the detention center, according to a former prisoner.

Moazzam Begg told CNN that, under the pressure of harsh questioning at Guantanamo Bay, he would have admitted to anything. He said it will be impossible to deliver justice for the suspected terrorists and alleged war criminals held there because any statements they made are inevitably compromised by the treatment used to secure them.

Begg, who spent nearly three years at Guantanamo, said he would have confessed to anything during interrogations. “What procedure can you use on people who have been systematically tortured including waterboarding, including being stripped naked and beaten? What sort of evidence can be admitted into a court of law that has been extracted under that process?” he asked.

The Obama administration has stated that waterboarding, a practice that creates the sensation of drowning, amounts to torture.

Begg, a British citizen, was seized during the war in Afghanistan and accused of supporting the Taliban government. His relatives have always insisted that he was wrongly identified. In 2005, the Bush administration returned him to Britain, and he was never charged.

On Wednesday, President Obama took further steps toward carrying out a campaign commitment to close the facility. Officials said the administration was preparing executive orders that would require the detention center to be shut down.

Earlier that day, a judge approved Obama’s request to pause prosecutions for 120 days while the cases of suspected terrorists were reviewed.

In his inaugural address, Obama emphasized that the country did not have to abandon justice in order to protect itself. “Our Founding Fathers, faced with perils we can scarcely imagine, drafted a charter to assure the rule of law and the rights of man, a charter expanded by the blood of generations. Those ideals still light the world, and we will not give them up for expedience's sake,” he said.

Legal problems are already affecting some of the most significant terrorism cases, including that of Mohamed al-Qahtani, described as the “20th hijacker.” He has been accused of helping plan, and possibly intending to take part in, the September 11, 2001, attacks.

Earlier this month, the retired judge responsible for deciding which Guantanamo prisoners should face trial before a U.S. military commission told The Washington Post that al-Qahtani had been tortured and therefore could not be prosecuted.

“Guantanamo Bay is the most notorious prison on earth,” Begg said. He added that he believes the prison serves as a source of radicalization for militants internationally.

Beyond the most prominent suspects, human rights advocates say there is very little evidence available to bring charges against dozens of detainees who remain imprisoned at Guantanamo. They argue that continuing to hold those men will not make it easier to contain al Qaeda.

“I think it's actually one of the most harmful myths about it, that we can't let people go because we've got the tiger by the tail,” said Cori Crider of the human rights group Reprieve.

Chris Arendt, a former Guantanamo Bay guard, said the Obama administration needs to reconsider and overhaul how it detains and tries future terrorism suspects, rather than simply closing Guantanamo.

“We're focused on this one camp that has become the star of the whole show. But there are camps everywhere,” he said. “There are camps in Iraq, in Afghanistan -- every country that American or the coalition forces have set their feet. None of those detainees are seeing any justice.”

Former Guantanamo Bay detainee Moazzam Begg has warned that the use of torture and coercive interrogation against prisoners at the U.S. detention facility has seriously compromised the evidence in many cases, creating major obstacles for any attempt to prosecute detainees fairly.

His comments come as the Obama administration moves forward with plans to close the Guantanamo Bay prison and review the status of those still held there. The facility, opened after the September 11 attacks, became one of the most controversial symbols of the United States’ “war on terror,” drawing criticism from human rights groups, lawyers, foreign governments and former prisoners who alleged unlawful detention, abuse and denial of due process.

Begg, a British citizen who was detained by U.S. forces and held at Bagram and Guantanamo before being released without charge, said that evidence obtained through mistreatment could not be trusted. He argued that statements made under torture, threats or extreme pressure are inherently unreliable because prisoners may say anything to stop the abuse or to satisfy interrogators.

According to Begg, this presents a profound legal and moral problem for the United States. If confessions or witness statements were extracted through abusive methods, they are unlikely to meet the standards required in civilian courts and may also be challenged in military proceedings. Such evidence, he said, should be considered inadmissible because it violates basic principles of justice.

The issue has become central to the Obama administration’s effort to determine what should happen to the remaining detainees. Some prisoners may be released or transferred, while others could face trial. But the legacy of interrogation practices used during the Bush administration has complicated those decisions. Prosecutors may find that key evidence is unusable, while defense lawyers are likely to argue that cases have been irreparably tainted.

Begg said the problem extends beyond individual prosecutions. In his view, Guantanamo has damaged the credibility of the United States and weakened its claims to uphold the rule of law. He suggested that unless the government fully confronts what happened there, including allegations of torture and abuse, the prison’s legacy will continue to cast doubt on American justice.

Human rights advocates have made similar arguments, saying that closing Guantanamo is only one step toward addressing the broader consequences of indefinite detention and coercive interrogation. They contend that the U.S. must also provide transparent legal processes, ensure accountability for abuses, and avoid relying on evidence obtained through unlawful methods.

The debate highlights one of the central dilemmas facing the Obama administration: how to protect national security while restoring confidence in the legal principles that Guantanamo came to represent as having been abandoned. For Begg and other critics, the answer lies in rejecting torture-tainted evidence and acknowledging that justice cannot be built on confessions obtained through fear, pain or coercion.

counterfactuals.output:
**Former Guantanamo detainee says torture could undermine prosecutions even if camp closes**

*By [Reporter Name], CNN-style report*

Former Guantanamo Bay detainee Moazzam Begg has warned that the use of torture and coercive interrogation at the U.S. detention facility could make it impossible to successfully prosecute some prisoners, even if President Barack Obama follows through on his pledge to close the camp.

Begg, a British citizen who was held by the United States for nearly three years without charge before being released in 2005, said evidence obtained through abusive treatment would likely be challenged in court and could be ruled inadmissible. That, he argued, would leave prosecutors struggling to build cases against detainees who have spent years in U.S. custody.

Obama has ordered the closure of the Guantanamo Bay detention camp, a facility that became one of the most controversial symbols of the Bush administration’s “war on terror.” But the administration faces difficult questions over what to do with the remaining detainees, including where they should be sent and whether they can be tried in civilian courts, military commissions or other legal forums.

Human rights groups and defense lawyers have long argued that harsh interrogation methods, secret detention and limited access to legal protections have compromised potential prosecutions. They say cases built on statements extracted under duress may collapse once subjected to judicial scrutiny.

Begg said the problem is not simply the location of the prison, but the legal legacy of what happened there. Closing Guantanamo, he argued, would not erase years of detention practices that damaged the credibility of evidence and the fairness of future trials.

U.S. officials have said they are reviewing detainee files individually to determine who can be prosecuted, transferred or released. But the process is expected to be complex, particularly in cases where evidence may be classified, unavailable, or tainted by allegations of mistreatment.

Guantanamo Bay opened in 2002 to hold foreign terrorism suspects captured after the September 11 attacks and during subsequent U.S.-led military operations. At its peak, the prison held nearly 800 detainees. Many were released without charge, while others remained in legal limbo for years.

Obama has said closing the facility is necessary to restore U.S. credibility and uphold the rule of law. Critics, however, have warned that moving detainees elsewhere will not resolve the central issues surrounding indefinite detention, admissible evidence and accountability for past abuses.

Begg’s warning underscores one of the most difficult challenges facing the administration: how to pursue justice in cases shaped by a detention system widely criticized for operating outside normal legal standards.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a full news report from London on Obama’s early moves to close Guantanamo, including quotes from former detainee Moazzam Begg, human rights advocates, and a former guard.
counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON —** President Barack Obama’s first moves to dismantle the detention system at Guantánamo Bay were welcomed in Britain on Thursday as a dramatic break with one of the most contentious policies of the Bush era, though former detainees and human rights campaigners warned that the test would be whether the prison is closed in fact — and not merely in name.

In one of his earliest acts as president, Obama ordered the U.S. detention facility at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, to be closed within a year and directed a review of the cases of the men still held there. The order declared that “the detention facilities at Guantánamo for individuals covered by this order shall be closed as soon as practicable, and no later than 1 year from the date of this order.”

The move was closely watched in London, where Guantánamo has long been a source of diplomatic tension and public anger. Several British citizens and residents were held there for years without trial, and campaigners have pressed successive British governments to seek the return or resettlement of former UK-based detainees.

Moazzam Begg, a British former detainee who was held at Bagram and Guantánamo before being released without charge in 2005, said Obama’s order marked an important symbolic shift but did not erase years of detention and alleged abuse.

Begg has repeatedly argued that closing Guantánamo must be accompanied by accountability, rehabilitation for former prisoners and an end to similar detention practices elsewhere. Speaking after Obama’s announcement, he described the decision as a welcome first step, but said the broader system that created Guantánamo also had to be confronted.

Human rights organisations echoed that caution. Amnesty International and other advocates said the closure order was overdue, but stressed that detainees must either be charged in fair civilian courts or released to countries where they would not face torture or persecution.

Campaigners also urged Washington not to transfer prisoners into a new form of indefinite detention under another name. They said the credibility of the new administration would depend on whether it rejected torture, secret detention and military commission trials that fell short of international standards.

“Closing Guantánamo is not the end of the story,” one London-based human rights advocate said. “The men held there need justice, not just a change of address. The world will be watching to see whether the United States restores due process or simply moves the problem somewhere else.”

The order also drew reaction from former U.S. military personnel who served at the prison. A former Guantánamo guard, who has since spoken publicly about his discomfort with the detention regime, said Obama’s decision acknowledged what many guards and service members had come to understand: that the prison had damaged America’s standing and placed troops in an impossible position.

“It became a symbol of everything that had gone wrong after 9/11,” the former guard said. “A lot of people who served there were told we were guarding the worst of the worst. Over time, it became clear that many of these men had never been given a real chance to answer the accusations against them.”

Obama’s order was part of a broader set of national security directives issued in the opening days of his presidency. He also moved to prohibit coercive interrogation techniques and ordered reviews of detention and interrogation policies, signalling a sharp reversal from the Bush administration’s approach to the “war on terror.”

The practical obstacles remain formidable. At the time of Obama’s announcement, roughly 240 men were still being held at Guantánamo. Some had been cleared for release but could not be safely returned to their home countries. Others were considered by U.S. officials to pose security risks, though evidence against them was often classified, disputed or potentially tainted by coercive interrogation.

European governments, including Britain, faced pressure to assist by accepting detainees who could not return home. British ministers had previously negotiated the return of UK nationals and some residents, but campaigners said London should do more to help close the prison.

Legal experts said the administration would need to decide quickly how to handle pending military commission cases and whether terrorism suspects would be prosecuted in federal courts. They also warned that the one-year deadline would be difficult to meet without sustained political support from Congress and cooperation from allies.

For former detainees, the announcement brought a mixture of relief and scepticism. Begg and other campaigners said the prison’s closure would be meaningful only if it was accompanied by transparency about what happened there and redress for those detained without charge.

“The orange jumpsuit, the cages and the legal black hole made Guantánamo infamous,” another advocate said. “But the real issue is whether any government can put people beyond the reach of law. Obama has taken an important first step. Now he has to prove that the rule of law applies even in cases involving national security.”

In London, where Guantánamo became a rallying point for anti-war protesters, Muslim community groups, lawyers and civil liberties organisations, the decision was seen as a rare moment of optimism after years of frustration.

But campaigners cautioned that the prison’s legacy would not disappear with the stroke of a presidential pen. The unanswered questions — who authorised abuse, how intelligence was obtained, what remedies former detainees would receive, and whether indefinite detention would continue elsewhere — remain central to the debate.

Obama’s order has raised expectations around the world. Whether he can meet them will depend on what happens next: the release or fair trial of detainees, the cooperation of allies, and the new administration’s willingness to confront the full legacy of Guantánamo.

counterfactuals.output:
**Guantanamo’s Legacy: Obama Administration Faces Legal Hurdles in Terror Cases**

*Washington (CNN) —* As the Obama administration moves to reshape U.S. detention and interrogation policy, one of the most difficult questions it faces is what to do with terrorism suspects whose cases were built during the most controversial years of the Bush administration’s war on terror.

At the center of the debate is the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba — a facility that became a global symbol of indefinite detention, harsh interrogation practices and legal uncertainty.

President Barack Obama entered office pledging to close Guantanamo and restore what he described as America’s commitment to the rule of law. But nearly seven years after the first detainees arrived at the prison, administration officials and prosecutors face a complicated problem: some suspects may be too dangerous to release, but too difficult to prosecute in traditional courts.

A major reason is the evidence.

In some cases, statements were obtained after detainees were subjected to harsh interrogation methods, including waterboarding — a practice the Obama administration has rejected as torture. In others, evidence may have been gathered through coercive questioning, prolonged isolation, or intelligence operations that cannot easily be revealed in open court.

Those problems could make prosecutions difficult, whether in federal court or before restructured military commissions.

Legal analysts say the government must now sort through years of detention files to determine which cases can stand up under rules that prohibit coerced testimony and require reliable evidence.

“The challenge is not simply whether someone is guilty,” one former military lawyer said. “It is whether the government can prove it in a way that meets American legal standards.”

The issue is especially sensitive in high-profile terrorism cases, including those involving alleged al Qaeda operatives accused of plotting attacks against the United States. Defense attorneys have argued that mistreatment in CIA custody and at Guantanamo tainted the evidence against their clients, making fair trials impossible.

Waterboarding remains one of the most politically charged aspects of the debate. The technique, which simulates drowning, was used on a small number of detainees held in secret CIA prisons. Bush administration officials defended the program as lawful and necessary to prevent attacks. Critics, including human rights groups and many legal experts, said it violated U.S. and international law.

Obama banned the practice shortly after taking office and ordered a review of interrogation policies. But ending the technique did not resolve the legal consequences of its use.

If prosecutors rely on statements made after harsh interrogations, defense lawyers are likely to argue those statements were coerced. Even evidence obtained later — under less aggressive questioning — could be challenged as the product of earlier abuse, a concept often described as “tainted evidence.”

That raises the possibility that some cases could collapse, or that judges could exclude key evidence.

The administration also faces political pressure from both sides. Civil liberties groups want detainees either charged in legitimate courts or released. Republicans and some Democrats warn that transferring Guantanamo prisoners to the United States could pose security risks and provoke public backlash.

Congress has also complicated the White House’s plans by raising objections to funding detainee transfers and demanding detailed plans for closing the prison.

For Obama, the legal dilemma underscores the broader legacy of Guantanamo: a detention system created in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks to operate outside the traditional criminal justice system, but one that has repeatedly been pulled back into the courts.

The Supreme Court has rejected several Bush-era arguments limiting detainees’ rights, ruling that Guantanamo prisoners may challenge their detention in U.S. courts. Those decisions forced the government to defend cases that were often assembled for intelligence purposes rather than prosecution.

Former officials say that distinction matters. Intelligence gathering is designed to disrupt plots and identify threats. Criminal prosecution requires admissible evidence, credible witnesses and procedures that can withstand judicial scrutiny.

Now, the Obama administration must decide how to handle detainees who fall between those two worlds.

Some may be tried in federal courts, where prosecutors have a record of winning terrorism convictions. Others could face military commissions, though the administration has sought changes to make those proceedings more credible. Still others may be transferred abroad if receiving countries agree to security conditions.

The hardest category involves detainees the government says remain dangerous but against whom usable evidence may be limited.

Human rights advocates argue that indefinite detention without trial would continue the very policies Obama promised to end. National security officials counter that releasing certain detainees could endanger U.S. interests.

The debate is likely to intensify as the administration reviews individual cases and attempts to meet its goal of closing Guantanamo. Each decision carries legal, political and security consequences.

For many observers, the prison’s legacy is no longer only about what happened there. It is about whether the United States can unwind a system built for wartime intelligence and fit it back into the framework of law.

As one legal scholar put it, “Guantanamo was easy to open in a moment of fear. Closing it — and dealing with the cases it produced — is proving far more difficult.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Obama Administration Moves to Suspend Guantanamo Military Commission Cases**

*Washington* — The Obama administration has moved to suspend proceedings in military commission cases at Guantanamo Bay, marking one of its first steps toward reshaping U.S. detention and terrorism policy after years of controversy surrounding the prison.

Military prosecutors requested a halt to pending commission cases, a pause that would allow the new administration to review the system used to try terrorism suspects held at the U.S. naval base in Cuba. The move follows President Barack Obama’s pledge to close Guantanamo and restore what he has described as America’s commitment to the rule of law.

Obama, who criticized the detention facility during his campaign, has argued that Guantanamo damaged the United States’ global standing and undermined confidence in the fairness of American justice. His administration is expected to examine whether detainees should be prosecuted in federal courts, military courts-martial, revised military commissions, or transferred to other countries.

The Guantanamo prison, opened in 2002 under President George W. Bush after the Sept. 11 attacks, became a central symbol of the U.S. war on terrorism. Supporters of the facility said it was necessary to hold dangerous terrorism suspects captured overseas. But human rights groups, foreign governments and legal critics condemned indefinite detention, coercive interrogation practices and limits placed on detainees’ ability to challenge their confinement.

Critics also argued that the prison became a propaganda tool for extremist groups, fueling anti-American sentiment and helping radicalize militants worldwide. They said images and reports from Guantanamo were used by jihadist organizations to recruit followers and portray the United States as hostile to Muslims and dismissive of international law.

The suspension of commission cases is likely to affect several high-profile prosecutions, including those involving detainees accused of involvement in major terrorism plots. Legal advocates welcomed the move as a sign that the administration intends to reassess a system they say lacked basic due process protections.

However, opponents warned that delaying the trials could complicate efforts to bring accused terrorists to justice and create uncertainty about the future of detainees considered too dangerous to release but difficult to prosecute.

Obama has said national security and constitutional principles need not be in conflict. The review of Guantanamo cases is expected to become an early test of that pledge, as the administration faces the challenge of dismantling a detention system that has defined much of the post-9/11 era while deciding what comes next for the men still held there.

**Original news-style segment transcript/article — not an actual CNN broadcast**

---

### **The Long Shadow of Guantanamo: Why Closing the Prison Remains So Difficult**

**ANCHOR:**  
More than two decades after the first detainees arrived at the U.S. military prison at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, the facility remains one of the most enduring and controversial symbols of the post-9/11 era.

Presidents from both parties have criticized it. Barack Obama signed an executive order to close it. Joe Biden’s administration continued efforts to reduce the detainee population. Human rights groups have called it a legal and moral failure. Yet Guantanamo remains open — weighed down by national security concerns, congressional restrictions, unresolved prosecutions, and the legacy of torture allegations that still shape the cases of men held there.

Tonight, we look at the challenges of closing Guantanamo, through the stories of detainees including **Mohamed al-Qahtani** and **Moazzam Begg**, and through warnings from rights organization **Reprieve** and former U.S. military personnel who served at the prison.

---

**CORRESPONDENT:**  
When the first detainees arrived at Guantanamo Bay in January 2002, they were brought hooded, shackled, and dressed in orange jumpsuits. The Bush administration argued the base was an essential facility for holding and interrogating suspected members of al Qaeda and the Taliban after the September 11 attacks.

At its height, Guantanamo held nearly 800 men. Most were eventually released or transferred without being charged with a crime. A much smaller number remain, including men facing prosecution before military commissions, men cleared for transfer but still awaiting resettlement, and others held under the laws of war.

But closing Guantanamo has proved far more complicated than simply shutting the gates.

One major obstacle is legal: Congress has repeatedly blocked the transfer of Guantanamo detainees to the United States, even for imprisonment or trial. Another is diplomatic: some detainees cannot safely be returned to their home countries because they may face torture, persecution, or instability. A third is the problem of prosecution itself — because evidence in some of the most serious cases is entangled with torture, coercive interrogations, and years of secret CIA detention.

Human rights advocates say that legacy has made justice harder, not easier.

---

### **Mohamed al-Qahtani and the Torture Allegations**

One of the most notorious cases is that of **Mohamed al-Qahtani**, a Saudi national once accused by U.S. officials of being intended as a possible “20th hijacker” in the September 11 attacks.

Al-Qahtani was captured in Afghanistan and transferred to Guantanamo. His interrogation became one of the clearest publicly documented examples of prisoner abuse at the facility.

According to government records and investigations, al-Qahtani was subjected to an intensive interrogation regime that included prolonged isolation, sleep deprivation, forced nudity, sexual humiliation, stress positions, threats, and other degrading treatment. He was reportedly interrogated for extended periods over weeks, under a special plan approved by senior officials.

In 2009, **Susan Crawford**, the senior Pentagon official overseeing the military commissions at the time, made a striking admission. She said the case against al-Qahtani could not proceed because his treatment met the legal definition of torture.

Her conclusion became a defining moment in the Guantanamo debate: one of the U.S. government’s own officials had acknowledged that torture had undermined a major terrorism prosecution.

Al-Qahtani was never tried. Years later, after psychiatric evaluations and legal proceedings, he was repatriated to Saudi Arabia for mental health treatment.

For critics of Guantanamo, his case shows how abusive interrogation practices did not merely violate human rights — they damaged the government’s ability to hold people accountable in court.

---

### **Moazzam Begg’s Account**

Another former detainee, **Moazzam Begg**, has become one of the best-known British voices describing life inside the post-9/11 detention system.

Begg, a British citizen, was detained in Pakistan in 2002 and later held at Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan before being sent to Guantanamo. He was released in 2005 without charge.

Begg has said he experienced and witnessed abuse during his detention, including threats, physical mistreatment, long periods of confinement, and psychological pressure. He has described being held in harsh conditions and separated from his family while never being formally tried.

His account has remained controversial in some circles because of broader debates over detainees, extremism, and national security. But his release without charge became part of a larger question: how did so many men end up imprisoned for years in a system where the normal rules of criminal justice did not apply?

For former detainees like Begg, the central issue is not only the physical conditions they endured, but the absence of due process — the sense that they were trapped in a legal black hole, with limited ability to challenge the accusations against them.

---

### **Reprieve’s Concerns**

The legal charity **Reprieve**, which has represented Guantanamo detainees and campaigned against the death penalty and secret detention, argues that the prison remains open because successive U.S. administrations have failed to fully confront the consequences of torture and indefinite detention.

Reprieve and other human rights organizations have raised several concerns:

- **Cleared men remain detained:** Some prisoners have been approved for transfer by U.S. review processes but remain at Guantanamo because no resettlement arrangement has been finalized.  
- **Torture complicates trials:** In the military commissions, especially in cases linked to the 9/11 attacks, years of litigation have focused on what evidence is tainted by torture and what the government must disclose about CIA black sites.  
- **Medical and psychological harm persists:** Many detainees are aging and have complex health needs after years of confinement, trauma, and uncertainty.  
- **Accountability remains limited:** Rights groups argue that while detainees have faced detention and prosecution, senior officials who authorized or enabled abusive interrogation policies have largely avoided legal consequences.  
- **Indefinite detention continues:** Some men remain held without charge under the theory that the U.S. is still engaged in an armed conflict against al Qaeda and associated forces.

Reprieve has warned that Guantanamo cannot simply be treated as a logistical problem. In its view, closure requires a reckoning with the policies that created the prison in the first place.

---

### **Former Guards Speak Out**

Some former Guantanamo guards have also raised concerns about what they saw and what the mission did to those assigned to carry it out.

Over the years, former military personnel who served at the prison have described a range of experiences. Some have defended their service, saying they followed lawful orders and guarded men they were told were dangerous. Others have spoken publicly about dehumanizing conditions, excessive force, psychological strain, and moral injury.

Several former guards have said the prison environment encouraged them to see detainees less as human beings than as threats. Some later expressed regret, saying they came to believe many detainees were not the “worst of the worst,” as officials originally claimed.

Their accounts add another layer to the debate: Guantanamo did not only affect detainees. It also affected the young service members ordered to guard them, many of whom were placed in a highly charged environment with limited understanding of who the prisoners were or why they were there.

---

### **Why Closing Guantanamo Is So Hard**

The obstacles to closing Guantanamo fall into several categories.

**First, politics.**  
For years, lawmakers have opposed bringing detainees to U.S. soil, arguing it would pose security risks. Even when presidents have wanted to close the prison, Congress has restricted funding for transfers into the United States.

**Second, security concerns.**  
Some released detainees have been accused of returning to militant activity, a point cited by opponents of closure. Supporters of closing the prison argue that risk can be managed through monitoring agreements, rehabilitation programs, and careful resettlement — and that indefinite detention without trial is not an acceptable solution.

**Third, the military commissions.**  
The cases against several high-profile detainees have moved slowly for years. Defense lawyers argue that torture and secret CIA detention must be fully examined before trials can proceed. Prosecutors argue they can use untainted evidence. The result has been a long-running legal stalemate.

**Fourth, resettlement.**  
Some detainees cannot return home. Others require countries willing to accept them, provide security assurances, and help them rebuild their lives. Those negotiations can take years.

**Fifth, the legacy of torture.**  
This may be the deepest problem. Torture allegations have weakened prosecutions, damaged U.S. credibility, and left unresolved questions about accountability. The treatment of men like Mohamed al-Qahtani remains central to why Guantanamo is not simply a prison, but a symbol.

---

**ANCHOR:**  
For supporters of Guantanamo, the facility has been a necessary tool in a dangerous era — a place to hold men accused of involvement with terrorist groups when traditional battlefields and criminal courts did not seem to fit.

But for critics, it represents a profound departure from the rule of law: indefinite detention, torture, secrecy, and cases that remain unresolved more than 20 years later.

The debate over closing Guantanamo is therefore not only about where to send the remaining detainees. It is about what the United States is prepared to acknowledge, what it is prepared to repair, and whether a system built outside ordinary legal boundaries can ever be cleanly dismantled.

More than two decades after it opened, Guantanamo Bay remains open — smaller than it once was, but still carrying the weight of the decisions made in the years after September 11.
